title: Inference tenancy risk and burst scoping intake
summary: Initial discovery to scope reserved GPU capacity, tenant isolation and burst strategy for Lattice Bio's production genomics inference workload. Customer emphasized strict data residency/VPC needs and wanted a hybrid reserved+burst model with on-demand fallback. Agreed next steps: security pack, cost estimate for reserved nodes + burst units, POC plan for 4-6 week bench, schedule detailed benchmark with sample payloads.
next_steps: Jordan to send security whitepaper and SOC2 docs (by 2025-09-13)
Sofia to draft POC plan and required sample dataset/benchmarks (by 2025-09-16)
Priya to provide expected QPS and p95 latency targets for 3 traffic tiers (by 2025-09-15)
Schedule benchmark call to run tokenized inference test (target week of 2025-09-22)
Pricing estimate for 4 reserved GPUs + burst package (Jordan, by 2025-09-18)
action_items: Jordan: share Private deployment architecture doc and SOC2/ISO excerpts - 2025-09-13
Sofia: create POC runbook + list of endpoints to test (including warmpool/prefix-caching tests) - 2025-09-16
Priya: export 1-week traffic trace and model sizes (quantized + fp16) - 2025-09-15
Dana: send compliance checklist (data residency, KMS, audit retention) - 2025-09-14
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-11
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Sofia Alvarez (Redwood SE), Liam O'Neill (RE), Amir R., Priya S., Dana L., Tom K.

Summary note: rough transcript with some transcription noise, occasional mishearings (K-V cash -> K V cache, SOM-2 -> SOC2, etc).

[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan, I'm the account lead on this – with Sofia and Liam who will do the technical deep dive. how are you all?
[00:10] Amir: good thanks, Amir here, head of ML at Lattice. appreciate you fitting us in.
[00:14] Priya: Priya, infra eng. i'll be owner for the POC and ops stuff.
[00:18] Dana: Dana, CISO. i'll be primarily on security and compliance.
[00:22] Jordan: great. quick agenda: understand your workload, isolation and residency constraints, burst profile, and then Sofia will sketch potential architectures and we can talk next steps. sound ok?
[00:31] Amir: yeah that's perfect. high level we run a genomics inference service – batched and single-query modes. model sizes vary 7B-70B depending on the pipeline. latency target for interactive queries is p95 < 400ms, for batch it's not strict but we want throughput. we'll likely deploy models behind our API, but we need strict tenant isolation since some runs touch PHI.
[00:49] Jordan: ok thanks. Priya, can you give us current infra?
[00:52] Priya: sure. right now we run most workloads on cloud instances, some self-hosted for dev. the inference load averages 150 qps during daytime, but spikes up to 1.2k qps during certain analysis windows. typical token length per request is 150-400 tokens. we have a steady background job load (batch) that needs GPU throughput but lower priority.
[01:14] Sofia: when you say 1.2k qps is that short single-shot queries or multi-turn chat?
[01:19] Amir: mostly single-shot scoring, so single forward passes. we do some streaming for longer sessions but that's smaller volume.
[01:25] Liam: and for the 7B to 70B models, do you quantize for prod or run FP16?
[01:30] Amir: we have a mix. smaller models are int8 quantized, larger ones we've trialed fp16 and int8-quantized variants. price sensitivity pushes us to use quantized where quality permits.
[01:39] Jordan: good notes. Dana, on the security/residency side?
[01:42] Dana: must be VPC-isolated, no model payloads leaving region X, KMS-managed keys, audit logs for all inference requests retained 90 days, and SOC2 + ISO27001 are non-negotiable. we prefer customer-managed keys if possible.
[01:58] Jordan: understood. Redwood has Dedicated (reserved GPU pools) and Private (VPC/on-prem) options; we can support customer KMS, and we publish SOC2 artifacts. Sofia, would you walk through architecture options?
[02:12] Sofia: sure. high-level there are three patterns we typically propose for a profile like this: 1) Dedicated-only: reserved GPUs in a private tenancy with node fencing and warm pools for prewarm; 2) Hybrid reserved + hosted-burst: reserved capacity handles baseline QPS, and we allow burst to Redwood hosted capacity via routed fallback; 3) Private/on-prem: full control, air-gapped if needed. each has tradeoffs.
[02:36] Amir: we want isolation but also don't want to overprovision for big spikes. hybrid seems interesting but can data/requests route to hosted? that violates our policy unless payloads are scrubbed.
[02:46] Sofia: you can configure routing policies so only non-sensitive workloads or anonymized payloads go to hosted. for fully sensitive flows we keep them on Dedicated or Private and we also support an encrypted prefix caching model so KV cache never leaves your VPC. small note: when I say KV cache some transcripts say K V cash lol.
[03:05] Priya: what's the latency impact of fallback to hosted?
[03:08] Sofia: it depends on region and model; hosted to region X will add typically 30–80ms network plus queuing, so p95 could jump. but the fallback path is useful for short spikes. we can also configure a small warmpool on Dedicated that automatically pre-warms additional nodes to avoid routing to hosted for short spikes.
[03:26] Amir: warmpool meaning prewarmed GPUs idle? what's the cost implication?
[03:30] Sofia: yes, warmpool are reserved nodes kept at low-cost prewarm state; cost is less than full reserved but more than pure burst-on-demand. pricing models are reserve + reduced warmpool charge + burst usage. Jordan can share numbers later.
[03:42] Jordan: yes i'll include a cost sketch. quick question: what percent of spikes are 5-10 min vs sustained hours?
[03:49] Priya: usually short, 5-30 minutes for ad-hoc runs, but sometimes a biweekly analysis window lasts 4-6 hours where throughput stays high.
[03:58] Sofia: so you need both prewarm for short spikes and capacity to handle sustained surge—auto-scaling rules can add nodes gradually, but for multi-hour surges it's cheaper to have reserved capacity.
[04:09] Amir: makes sense. on the isolation side we need strong tenant separation. are there features for tenant fencing?
[04:15] Liam: yes we have node-level tenant fencing where reserved nodes are pinned to your account; multi-tenancy is prevented via hypervisor level and runtime enforcement. we also support per-tenant quotas and hard isolation for Dedicated.
[04:28] Dana: and for audit/logging? can we ship raw request logs to our SIEM? retention policies?
[04:33] Sofia: we support syslog/S3 export and an audit log API. retention configurable, default 30 days but can increase to 365 for enterprise. we can integrate with customer SSO and SAML for RBAC.
[04:46] Dana: KMS integration? customer-managed?
[04:49] Jordan: yes, customer-managed keys via our KMS integration for both Private and Dedicated. Private on-prem can use HSM if needed.
[04:57] Amir: ok great. on performance: can we run a benchmark where we replay our QPS trace with token distributions? we want to measure p50/p95/p99 and cost-per-token for quantized vs fp16 models.
[05:07] Sofia: definitely. for meaningful results we'll need sample payloads, model binaries or model configs, and a representative traffic trace. we'll run dedicated reserved nodes and compare results with the hosted fallback path and with quantized builds.
[05:20] Priya: noted, i'll get you the traffic trace plus the list of models. question on prewarming: how fast can warmpool spin up into production?
[05:26] Liam: warmpool prewarm time depends on model size and kernel compile time; for 7B models it's usually < 90s, for 70B could be several minutes if compilation needed. we recommend keeping warmpool for large models if you need sub-2min spin up.
[05:41] Amir: is compilation deterministic? we saw wide variance with other runtimes.
[05:44] Sofia: compilation depends on sequence length and kernel selector; we have a caching layer for compiled kernels so repeat starts are much faster. initial warmup is the slow bit.
[05:53] Dana: on compliance, if we use hybrid and route some content to hosted, will the hosted logs contain any identifying tokens? how do you guarantee no PHI leaves?
[06:01] Jordan: that's a policy plus technical config. you can tag routes as 'no-hosted fallback' for flows carrying PHI. for other flows you can scrub sensitive fields client-side before sending. we can also run the PII scrubber as an optional step in your VPC.
[06:16] Amir: ok. switching to sizing: we need help sizing reserved units. our baseline is 150 qps, occasional 1.2k spikes. how to translate to GPUs?
[06:24] Sofia: depends heavily on model and batch profile. rough back-of-envelope: a 7B int8 model can do 300-600 qps per A100-equivalent GPU depending on batching; a 70B fp16 might do 10-30 qps. so mix matters. if you standardize on an int8 13B model for many paths, 4 reserved GPUs could handle baseline with some headroom, warmpool for short spikes, and burst to hosted for the tail. but we should size after benchmark replay.
[06:53] Priya: so suggested starting reserve is 4 GPUs? what about regional redundancy and failover?
[06:58] Liam: we recommend at least 2 AZs for Dedicated to avoid single-AZ failure; traffic routing and warmpool across AZs for resilience. failover adds cost but necessary for SLA.
[07:12] Dana: SLA expectations? do you provide latency and uptime SLAs for Dedicated?
[07:16] Jordan: yes Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and committed latency SLOs for reserved nodes; specifics depend on contract level. we'll include draft SLA language.
[07:25] Amir: what's the typical POC timeline? we want to validate throughput and isolation and then decide in about 6 weeks.
[07:30] Sofia: our standard POC is 4-6 weeks: week 1 infra onboarding + security review, week 2 model/bench setup, week 3 runs and tuning, week 4 evaluation and handoff. extended runs for longer load profiles add 1-2 weeks.
[07:43] Priya: onboarding effort? how much infra work on our side?
[07:46] Liam: for Dedicated you need a VPC peering and some routing rules, and customer KMS if using CMK. for Private on-prem there's more setup, but we have an on-prem engineer to assist. most customers can be live within 1-2 weeks for a sandbox.
[07:59] Amir: ok. any red flags we should know? I mean operationally – preemption, noisy neighbors?
[08:05] Sofia: with reserved Dedicated nodes pinned to your tenancy, noisy neighbor risk is zero. preemption only in on-demand nodes; reserved are stable. for hybrid burst to hosted you'd share multi-tenant hosts so that path has multi-tenant behavior.
[08:19] Priya: what's the monitoring surface? token-level cost, per-route latency, traces?
[08:23] Jordan: Redwood Console shows per-route token/latency breakouts, trace hooks, and per-model dashboards. we can also ship metrics to your telemetry.
[08:31] Dana: any gaps on encryption at rest and in transit?
[08:34] Sofia: data in transit is TLS, at rest is encrypted with customer-managed keys for Dedicated/Private. We also offer field-level encryption if requested.
[08:43] Amir: great. cost: how do you price warmpool? example numbers would be helpful.
[08:48] Jordan: I'll send a sketch but example: reserved monthly + warmpool incremental hourly rate + burst per-second usage for hosted. exact numbers depend on GPU class and region. we'll include an example for 4 reserved A100-eqs + 2 warmpool nodes + baseline burst assumption.
[09:05] Priya: one more technical detail: KV caching and prefix caching—do you store caches in customer VPC?
[09:10] Liam: for Dedicated and Private yes, we can store prefix/KV caches inside your VPC and avoid shared caches. hosted path uses our global cache. that's configurable per-route.
[09:21] Amir: and cold-start behavior with KV: if cache miss occurs are you pulling from centralized store? that adds latency?
[09:26] Sofia: cache misses will cause runtime to do full forward; KV cache is local to the serving node where possible, but for cache miss we can fall back to the model. that's where warmpool helps reduce misses.
[09:36] Dana: any compliance attestations you can share now?
[09:39] Jordan: yes, i'll attach SOC2 report summary in the follow-up. Dana: thanks.
[09:45] Amir: ok, i want to circle back to burst failover policies. is there a way to set hard thresholds, e.g., if p95 > 450ms we stop routing to hosted or throttle?
[09:54] Sofia: yes, routing policies are policy-driven and can use metrics. you can set automations: if p95 > X, disable hosted fallback, or route to a smaller model variant. you can also set cost-based guards.
[10:07] Priya: model variants – is it straightforward to keep a smaller quantized model as fallback?
[10:11] Liam: yes model aliasing and automatic fallback to variants is supported. we can run canary rollouts to verify quality.
[10:18] Amir: perfect. any security concerns about model variant fidelity? we need to ensure fallback doesn't produce bad outputs for clinical work.
[10:26] Sofia: that's why we recommend running a set of eval prompts as part of POC and set quality gates. Redwood Optimize can monitor regressions against those evals and trigger alerts.
[10:37] Jordan: good. nearing the middle of the call — let's capture concrete next steps. Jordan will share security docs and pricing sketch; Sofia will draft POC runbook; Priya will share traffic trace and model configs; Dana will send compliance checklist.
[10:52] Amir: agreed. any blockers to start the POC?
[10:55] Dana: just need to confirm legal/contract; we'll need a DPA and data processing terms.
[11:01] Jordan: legal will prepare a DPA template; we can fast-track standard terms.
[11:05] Priya: ok timeline wise we should be able to start the week of 2025-09-22.
[11:10] Sofia: we'll aim to have a sandbox ready within 5 business days after we get the onboarding checklist.
[11:16] Amir: one last question — does Redwood support per-request redaction plugin? we want to scrub PHI client-side but also have server-side scrub as defense in depth.
[11:25] Liam: yes there's a server-side optional PII scrubber, but best practice is client-side first. we can demo both in the POC.
[11:32] Dana: and can audit logs be non-reversible? we need write-once retention for certain logs.
[11:37] Sofia: we can configure WORM-like sinks to S3 with lifecycle rules—will need legal to sign off.
[11:44] Jordan: ok, unless there are other questions let's open the floor for any technical deep dive requests.
[11:49] Amir: can we dig a bit into exact GPU types supported? we use A100 today, but interested in newer Ampere/Carbon classes if available.
[11:56] Liam: we support A100-equivalent, H100 where available, and have accelerated kernels for newer Ampere series. pick depends on cost vs perf. we'll include perf profiles.
[12:07] Priya: nice. any constraints around IP for custom kernels?
[12:10] Sofia: we own the runtime but we can provide determinist runbooks; custom kernel changes are engineering-assisted with the appropriate IP terms in the contract.
[12:19] Amir: ok that's fine.
[12:21] Jordan: cool — let's recap: deliverables and owners on timeline.
[12:26] [recap and next steps repeated briefly — aligns with the metadata action items].
[12:40] Dana: thanks, this was useful.
[12:42] Jordan: thanks everyone. we'll follow up with docs and schedule the bench.
[12:46] Amir: thanks. bye.

(End of meeting)
